lesson.title: Health Care for a Nation: Medicare and Medicaid
lesson.summary: Signed into law in 1965 as amendments to the Social Security Act, Medicare provided health insurance for older Americans while Medicaid extended coverage to many low-income Americans, together marking the largest expansion of the federal government's role in health care up to that point.
lesson.body:
The idea of national health insurance in the United States dates back decades before the Great Society. President Harry Truman had proposed a form of universal health coverage in the 1940s, but it went nowhere amid opposition from the American Medical Association and widespread fears of what critics called "socialized medicine." The Great Society revived the idea in a more limited form, targeting the two groups seen as most vulnerable and, politically, most sympathetic: the elderly and the poor.

On July 30, 1965, in Independence, Missouri, President Johnson signed the bill establishing Medicare and Medicaid as amendments to the Social Security Act of 1935, the same law that had created federal retirement pensions during the New Deal. In a symbolic gesture honoring Truman's earlier advocacy, Johnson signed the bill in Truman's presence and presented him with the first Medicare card.

Medicare, established under Title XVIII of the Social Security Act, provides federally funded health insurance to Americans aged sixty-five and older regardless of income, later extended to certain younger people with disabilities. Medicaid, under Title XIX, is a joint federal-state program that provides health coverage to low-income individuals and families, with eligibility rules and administration varying somewhat from state to state.

Together, these programs marked a major expansion of the New Deal era's social insurance model, applying its central idea, that the federal government should guarantee a baseline of economic security, to health care as well. Both programs grew enormously in scope over the following decades and remain central, and often politically contested, pillars of American social policy today.
